text: The assembly will now turn to agenda
item eight entitled general debate.
I will now make a statement as the
president of the general assembly.
Excellencies,
Mr. Secretary General,
former presidents of the General
Assembly,
ladies and gentlemen,
40 years ago, I stood in this very hall
as a newly minted member of the cabinet
of the 41st President of the General
Assembly, Mr. Human Rashid Chri. at that
time. He said, and I quote, "In recent
years, there appears to have been a
crisis of confidence in the United
Nations itself. There is a general
feeling that the United Nations today
needs revitalizing in a number of
aspects in order to bring it into line
with the priorities of a changing
world."
That was 40 years ago.
Questions about multilateralism
and the effectiveness of the United
Nations therefore are not new.
They have been part of this place since
the first stone was led. Yet through it
all, the United Nations has persevered.
Not because it is perfect, but because
it is irreplaceable
and because the alternative is simply
unfathomable.
The world of 1945 was imperial.
The second world war, the colossal
devastation wrought by it and the
holocaust left humanity bankrupt morally
and fiscally. Something had to change
and this place was that change. It
ushered in a long era of diplomacy which
continues member states coming together
to work through their problems because
they knew that the alternative guns
blazing and bombs dropping simply was
not an option. Perhaps the clearest
evidence of its achievements is here in
this very hall. In 1945,
50 nations participated in the San
Francisco conference. Today, eight
decades later, the organization has
193 member states. The UN has brought
together humanity under one roof. This
is unprecedented in human history. The
core promise of this institution is
and remains to prevent the unimaginable
a third world war. The fact that we have
avoided such calamity is among the
greatest achievements this institution
could ever deliver.
But survival alone cannot be our sole
measure of success. Outside these walls,
people are not asking whether the United
Nations still exists. They are asking
whether it works. Yes, there have been
wars and conflicts that we could not
prevent and issues we could not resolve.
The Palestinian issue continues
unresolved for decades. As the secretary
general
just alluded to, wars and conflict and
their aftermath are ravaging Sudan,
Gaza, Ukraine, Myanmar, and the Middle
East. But even as those wars raged, the
United Nations stayed and served. I have
seen it up close in my own country,
Bangladesh, where the United Nations
country team in Coxes Bazar is striving
to do more with less to support Rohingya
refugees in the camps who are yearning
to return back to Myanmar. Just
recently, a representative from a war
torn nation said to me, "Your
peacekeepers from Bangladesh were not
just blue helmets. They built roads and
communities. They fed children. They
helped rebuild societies and put us on
the road to proper governance. In Iraq,
the United Nations system helped nearly
5 million people return home. It
rehabilitated hundreds of schools,
electricity stations, and water
treatment plants. And right now in
Haiti, the entire United Nations family
is delivering amid immense security and
governance challenges. These stories
rarely made make headlines. But we
should never lose sight of what it is
that is working.
At the same time, let us not turn a
blind eye to where we have fallen short,
particularly in a world where challenges
seem to multiply by the day and newer
challenges appear every day. The war in
Gaza has left over 70 pe,000 people
dead, including thousands of children.
Humanitarian support has been a fraction
of what is needed. The ongoing wars
across Middle East and Europe have
consequences far beyond their front
lines. And the heartbreaking natural
disaster in Nepal and China was not just
an isolated event, but yet another
horrible climax to our collectively in
insufficient response to climate change.
The circumstances and the politics of
this crisis differ. But our commitment
under under the United Nations charter
do not. The principles of
multilateralism,
international law, international
humanitarian law, the protection of
civilians and humanit humanitarian
access cannot be applied selectively.
Not if we want the world to trust us.
It is precisely at such times that we
must honestly confront our setbacks our
however profound not with blame,
cynicism or blind hope but with action,
sober reflection, cleareyed realism and
pragmatism.
This is how we charge these turbulent
waters and this is what we need to
reveal trust in this institution. The
central focus of this session and my
statement. So how do we build back
trust?
Trust is not given, it is earned. And we
earn trust I believe in three ways.
First by being unapologetically
realistic about where we are falling
behind. Second, by taking a foundational
look at the reforms of the United
Nations to deliver better. And third, by
making our in work inclusive and
engaging all relevant stakeholders uh
from all parts of our society.
Let me elaborate
on my first point. We must be frank
about where the challenges lie and what
needs to be fixed even when the
necessary changes may prove painful.
Consider peace and security one of the
pillars of the organizations. Under the
UN charter, the security council bears
primary responsibility for the
maintenance of international peace and
security. Yet when the council is unable
to act, member states turn to the
general assembly. We saw this as early
as 1950 with uniting for peace
resolution and we have seen it more
recently through the assembly's veto
initiative. These two principles or
principal organs of our organization are
complimentary not competing. The charter
provides for an appropriate balance
between them. Both chambers must do
their respective part. To be fair, the
security council when it acts proves its
strength and effectiveness. It helped
liberate Kuwait, ended civil war in El
Salvador, supported Namibia's
independence, led rebuilding of
Colombia,
Cambodia, and stabilized conflict
affected countries through peacekeeping.
Yet, when the council is unable to act
on important matters, the effectiveness
of our organization as a whole is called
into question. In 1945,
humanity placed its trust in the council
in good faith, giving it the
extraordinary responsibility of
maintaining international peace and
security. The council accepted that
responsibility and entered into a
compact. It must now hold up its its end
of the bargain. This is what the people
of the world expects. And in their eyes,
when the security council works, the
United Nations works. The promise of
1945 still binds us today. I call on the
Security Council and all of its members
to step up to lead as we needed to lead
and to act when we needed to act. Linked
to this is the question of security
council reform. I will support General
Assembly intergovernmental negotiations
in its work to make the council more
representative, transparent and
reflective of the geopolitical realities
of our time. Ensuring fair
representation for underrepresented
regions must remain a priority.
As the secretary general has said,
nowhere is this more important right now
than in Africa. After eight decades, the
largest region by number of member
states and a key focus of UN
peacekeeping remains under reppresented
on the security council. Africa needs to
be at the table, not on the menu. Africa
cannot be asked to wait indefinitely for
the rightful place on the council.
Ending Africa's under representation now
is a question of fairness, justice, and
ultimately the credibility of this
organization.
Turning to the development pillar and
particularly the sustainable development
goals, we are right to focus on the
challenges. Last year, OECD donors spent
about
175 billion on development assistance, a
whopping 23% drop year on year. And yet,
military expenditures approached $3
trillion, capping 11 straight years of
growth. All the while progress on the
SDGs stalled at just over a third of
targets and developing countries are now
paying the price for supply chain
disruptions.
Disruptions they did not cause and
cannot cure. The contrasts could not be
more stark. We must better prioritize on
how we spend our resources by augmenting
development assistance, addressing debt
burdens, reforming the international
financial architecture, fulfill
fulfilling our Civia and Paris
commitments
and implementing the programs of actions
for least developed countries, landlock
developing countries and small island de
developing states as well as African
Union's agenda 2063
because where we have done so. The
results are clear. Over the past decade,
nearly 1 billion people have gained
access to safe safely managed drinking
water. Electricity now reaches 92% of
world's population very close to
universality and internet access has
risen from 40% to 74%.
Behind these numbers are healthier
children, more resilient communities,
greater opportunities for women and
girls, and renewed hope. These gains
show that accelerating the SDGs is
possible when
developing countries and the development
partners work in concert and this is
indeed a share responsibility.
Developing countries must also intensify
their own efforts through domestic
resource mobilization and plug any
leakage of or corruption, including
capital flight, a plague that until
recently undermined development in my
own country under a repressive and
authoritarian regime.
Turning to human rights, we should
acknowledge that these are central to
the other two pillars. They can promote
peace. There cannot be there cannot be
peace without rights and advance
sustainable development. And we
recognize one of the most urgent
assaults on human dignity today, hate
speech that incites violence.
It is a growing threat to regional and
global peace and it is on the rise.
Hateful narratives are spreading like
wild wildfire across borders and into
homes at unprecedented speed and scale.
They target women and girls, minorities,
migrants, refugees, and persons with
disabilities, often for political gain.
New and emerging technologies are used
to amplify lies, manipulate public
debate, spread hatred, and give
incitement to violence faster and
farther than ever before. We must choose
dialogue and tolerance and foster a
culture in which human rights are
respected not only in law but in our
daily interactions. And we must stop
cherrypicking of those rights that fit
our respective cultures or politics of
the day. Whether it is Islamophobia,
anti-semitism, homophobia, misogyny,
it's all the same. Hatred repackaged and
relabeled. Let us use the tools of our
age not to deepen fear but to widen
understanding and advance human dignity
for everyone everywhere.
My second point making the United
Nations fit for the future which
requires a more foundational approach to
reform.
The UN80 initiative is a constructive
start. Thank you Mr. Secretary General
for this. But it is only a start. Moving
positions on a budget sheet may deliver
savings. Margaring or renaming bodies
may reduce duplication. Streamlining
structures may improve efficiency. These
steps are important and often essential
for good housekeeping, but they are not
enough. We need to dig deeper to address
the problems beneath the superructure
because the United Nations reform
challenges are chronic and fundamental.
On 24th November 1949,
barely four years after the founding of
the United Nations, this assembly
adopted resolution 310
Roman 4 entitled problem of
proliferation and overlapping of
programs of the United Nations and of
the specialized agencies. It urged
member states and I quote to refrain
from initiating new projects other than
those which are urgently required and
which can be effectively carried out.
Yet we have not paid sufficient
attention to our own decision. We have
since created thousands of mandates of
which 4,000 are still active
irrespective of whether they were
required or could be effectively carried
out. We cannot continue treating a
chronic ailment with temporary
painkillers when what we need is a
deeper diagnosis and a more profound
plan for transformation even if that
plan proves painful.
And here I must be equally candid. This
will happen only if member states take
charge. Time and again we say that
United Nations reforms must be memberled
which looks like a tacit admission that
they are not.
Too often we member states fail to take
the wheel. Passive ownership is not
enough. If we do not claim proactive
ownership of this place we cannot expect
expect it to selfheal. So let us engage.
Let us take charge. Fix our own house.
respect sovereignty of member states and
together deliver the transformation we
need.
As we decide what must change, we must
also recognize what already works. Again
and again, member states tell us that
the United Nations works well at the
country level, emergency situations, and
in keeping and building peace. We should
build on that success. We should
strengthen the United Nations work in
these areas and draw increasingly on
local capacity including qualified
national institutions and individuals
including women and young people. We
should ensure that all activities at the
country level from development support
to peacekeeping and are properly
integrated and produce the highest
synergy. We should we should ensure
avoidance of tariff battles among
different parts of the UN and exercise
care to select the leaders at the
country level that are fit to lead. We
want to have full value for money. Let's
remember we the the organization
financial viability remains a chronic
concern. We must ensure that it receives
sufficient resources on a sustained
basis and that all countries paid their
dues on time and we without conditions.
We should also recognize that dues to
the United Nations come from hardworking
place all around the world. Every penny
must therefore be therefore be properly
accounted for. Every penny must be
invested to achieve impact on the ground
for the people we serve.
The role of the member states supported
by the secretariat is essential to
delivering our work but not sufficient.
This brings me to my third point.
Building a more open and inclusive
United Nations. We know that the United
Nations of today and the world it serves
are profoundly different from those of
Nowhere the the pace of change more is
more evident today than in artificial
intelligence. AI can be a powerful
accelerator of human progress.
Therefore, we must not close the door to
innovate in innovation. At the same
time, we must address AI's potential
harms, including job losses and widening
of the digital divide. We cannot also
rule out the possibility that AI,
particularly artificial general
intelligence or AGI, could affect the
very human survival.
That demands prudent and reliable guard
rails based on scientific evidence to
safeguard the global public interest
while allowing innovation to go forward.
Governments must remain at the heart of
this endeavor. But governments do not
have a monopoly on expertise, capital,
technology, innovation or influence.
Much of that experience and capacity
already lies with businesses,
innovators, civil society and others. We
need to keep the doors of United Nations
unlocked to the those developing and
using AI not someday now. And we are
falling further as we are falling
farther behind each day. AI differs from
earlier proliferation challenges in one
critical respect. It is already embedded
in nearly every facet of our lives in
our water systems, electricity grids,
economies and militaries. We cannot
allow an arms race for control of AI to
carry us over the precipice. There is
clear precedent for the United Nations
engagement with worldchanging
developments. We did so on nuclear
non-prololiferation
through the Montreal protocol to protect
the ozen layer and with the United
Nations declaration on human cloning in
We need experts, innovators, industry
leaders, scientists, civil society and
academia all working together with
member states on these issues of our
times.
Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, we
have an opportunity in this session to
show that we have learned from what
works, that we are prepared to confront
what does not, and that we can build a
United Nations capable not simply of
surviving change, but of shaping change.
To seize that opportunity, we must be
realistic enough to confront hard
truths, bold enough to reform, and
inclusive enough to bring the right
people to the table. That is how in my
view we will renew trust in our
organization and make it fit for future.
The task is not easy nor can it be done
overnight. Then we must persist over the
long haul. 81 years ago, President
Truman expressed the hope that the
United Nations would endure for nine
decades. Here we are at the beginning of
the UN's ninth decade. Let us dedicate
ourselves to the task of rebuilding
trust and confidence in the in the
United Nations so that it lives up to
the incredible potential for me for for
many decades to come. I thank you.
